--- Auto Summary (generated, may be imperfect) ---
Redwood ran through JSON structured output and function-calling capabilities, demoed guardrails in the Console, touched on Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization, and discussed dedicated vs hosted and VPC options. Action items: pricing/pilot, benchmark, security pack.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, account exec at Redwood. With me is Liam, our solutions engineer, who will walk through structured output and function-calling. Who do we have on the BlueHorizon side?
[00:08] Priya Kapoor: Hi Maya, Priya here. I'm head of ML. We've got Daniel, Sara, Tom and Elena on the call as well.
[00:12] Daniel Ortiz: hey.
[00:14] Sara Kim: hey all.
[00:18] Liam Patel: Awesome. Quick agenda — we'll do a short intro, demo JSON mode / function calling in the Console and API, show how you can anchor schemas and guardrails, then cover Optimize suggestions and discuss deployment patterns (hosted, dedicated, private).
[00:29] Priya Kapoor: Great, our main use case is structured extraction from customer emails and then firing a downstream fulfillment API — so the output must be strict JSON, validated, and we need to call internal tools to create tickets.
[00:40] Liam Patel: Perfect, that's exactly what function-calling + structured output is designed for. We'll show a schema-first approach so model emits the right keys and types; then we'll demo tool calling (we map a function spec to your ticketing API).
[00:51] Tom Reyes: Quick security note — we run in VPC and need to ensure KMS and customer-managed keys, plus audit logs. Also latency targets are tight for the fast path.
[01:03] Elena Costa: And SOC2 / ISO compliance requirements — can you include network diagrams and your SOC2 report?
[01:09] Maya Chen: Absolutely — we'll include the compliance pack. We'll also show how Dedicated or Private deployments let you use your KMS and VPC.

[03:05] Liam Patel: Alright jumping into Console. (screen share) So here's the Redwood Console, route config at the top — you can toggle JSON mode which pins the model to emit structured output according to the schema we paste here.
[03:20] Liam Patel: I'll paste a sample JSON schema — note: types, required fields, and pattern constraints. The Console will validate candidate outputs and surface schema mismatches.
[03:35] Liam Patel: Example: order_id as string, items as array of objects with sku, qty as int, and customer_notes as optional string. We can also add enumerations to constrain values.
[04:00] Daniel Ortiz: How strict is the enforcement? If the model emits extra fields, will Redwood strip them or fail the request?
[04:07] Liam Patel: Good question. You have two options — strict mode which rejects responses that don't conform (useful for pipelines), or tolerant mode where we map and then run post-validators and optionally run a repair step. In strict mode we return a structured error so your app can decide fallback logic.
[04:25] Maya Chen: This is where guardrails come in — you can configure fallback to a simpler model or run a deterministic extractor on schema failure.
[04:36] Priya Kapoor: And for calling our ticket API, do you expose a function spec?
[04:40] Liam Patel: Yes — function calling maps to an OpenAPI-ish function signature. We send the structured payload as the function args, and Redwood can either call the external endpoint from the managed plane (hosted) or emit the function call for your client to execute (private/deployed).
[04:57] Sara Kim: What's the difference between calling from managed plane vs client execute? Concerned about PII leaving our environment.
[05:05] Maya Chen: If you're using Private or Dedicated within your VPC, calls can be routed over a private link and use your KMS. For hosted, we can work with a redaction step or only emit the function call and let your infra perform the final call.
[05:20] Elena Costa: Ok that's important, we prefer emit-for-client-execute for now.

[06:45] Liam Patel: Now I'll switch to API mode — same schema passed in the request body as json_schema param. Demo request.. (types) Sending a sample email prompt.
[07:05] [audio gap / short pause]
[07:12] Liam Patel: Response streaming coming in — see how tokens stream and we get a function call event with name create_ticket and args payload as strict JSON. Note: transcription sometimes shows 'KV cash' instead of 'KV cache' — we're aware of common mis-hearings in transcripts.
[07:35] Priya Kapoor: That event model is exactly what we need. For retries and idempotency, can we include a deterministic ticket_id in the schema?
[07:43] Liam Patel: Yes, you can include an id field and set it as required. For idempotency we also recommend Redwood's dedupe middleware or attach a client-generated id as part of headers.

[10:00] Liam Patel: Switching to guardrails — Console lets you define rules: block if PII looks like SSN patterns, rewrite if confidence below threshold, or augment ratings. These rules run pre- or post-model. Also we show how Optimize suggests quantization or batch sizing based on your token distribution.
[10:28] Maya Chen: Quick note on Optimize — for high throughput invoice parsing you likely want batching + prefix KV cache. Optimize will suggest a quantization profile (int8 or int4 depending on quality SLO) and a recommended hardware SKU.
[10:46] Tom Reyes: What's the observed latency penalty for int4 quant vs FP16 on your runtime? We need p95 under 300ms for the fast path.
[10:54] Liam Patel: Typical numbers: FP16 on A100 gives ~180–220ms p95 for small sequences; int8 can add 10–20ms overhead during decoding but reduces cost substantially. For p95 under 300ms we can recommend specific kernel choices and batching config. We'll run a quick benchmark.

[13:15] Daniel Ortiz: Does Redwood support function calling chaining? eg. call enrichment service then ticketing?
[13:22] Liam Patel: Yes, you can chain calls — we model function outputs and they can be fed as subsequent inputs, or orchestrate via Redwood's route rules. Caution: chain length affects latency and cost.

[15:00] Priya Kapoor: Can we attach RBAC to routes so only product ops can trigger the ticketing route?
[15:06] Maya Chen: Definitely — RBAC is part of the Console. You can scope tokens to specific routes and models, and we integrate with SSO (SAML/SCIM) for enterprise accounts.

[18:30] Liam Patel: Demoing a guardrail failure: I'll force a bad output by giving ambiguous prompt. (types) see, Console flags schema mismatch and returns an error object with code schema_validation_failed and a snippet of the model output to help debugging. We also show how to auto-run a repair function that invokes a deterministic extractor and retries the model if needed.
[19:05] Sara Kim: How do we version schemas? We'll need schema evolution as we add fields.
[19:12] Liam Patel: Each route has a schema registry in Console — you can create versions and pin a route to a schema version. Rollouts can be canaryed: 10% traffic uses new schema/model, we surface regression metrics in Console.

[22:05] Liam Patel: Now quick note on telemetry — token-level cost, per-route latency breakdowns, and error rates are all in Console. You can link traces back to individual requests for debugging.
[22:18] Tom Reyes: For audit, can we export raw logs and have them delivered to our SIEM?
[22:23] Maya Chen: Yes, we support log delivery (S3, GCS) and syslog/ELK integrations; audit logs include request metadata but payload delivery can be redacted per your policy.

[25:00] Liam Patel: Let's pivot to Optimize recommendations — here's a sample ML workload analysis. Based on your expected sequence lengths (most emails ~200 tokens) Optimize suggests a mid-sized quantized variant and batching window of 50–100ms to balance latency and throughput. You can also pin a model family and let the router fallback to cheaper variants under load.
[25:40] Priya Kapoor: If we run a pilot, what's the recommended scope? We want to test end-to-end — extraction, guardrails, function call to ticketing, and latency under load.
[25:51] Maya Chen: Typical pilot: 2–4 weeks, 10k–50k requests, we run benchmarks, provide a Dedicated trial or Private demo depending on security. We'll provide a pilot SOW; pilot includes a benchmark run, integration support and a dedicated SE.

[28:10] Daniel Ortiz: Cost — how do you break down costs? We need per-ticket cost estimate including downstream compute.
[28:18] Maya Chen: Main cost levers: model size/profile, tokens per request, and replication for latency. Optimize helps estimate per-token cost; for function calling also account for extra tokens for function signature. We'll share a spreadsheet with modeled costs for your volumes.

[30:40] Liam Patel: Live API example: calling the create_ticket function. (types) here's the payload — small imperfection in name transcribed as 'Jon' instead of 'John' in the sample, shows typical transcription fuzz; we recommend canonicalization rules.
[31:05] Priya Kapoor: Do you support custom canonicalizers? We have customer names that need normalization.
[31:10] Liam Patel: Yes, you can plug in deterministic post-processors in the route pipeline or run a small microservice that receives the function call event and normalizes before final persist.

[33:50] Elena Costa: Security — again, we need to review encryption at rest, KMS integration, and perf implications of customer-managed keys.
[33:58] Maya Chen: For Dedicated/Private you can bring your own KMS/HSM; there's minimal perf impact for keys used at connection time, but per-object encryption can have overhead. We'll include the network diagram and SOC2 report in the pack.

[36:00] Liam Patel: One last Console feature — you can create test suites (prompt sets) with expected outputs; Console will run regression evals on new model versions and alert on metric drift (fidelity, schema passes). That ties into your QA.
[36:20] Sara Kim: That's perfect — we need regression detection for schema breakages.

[38:00] Maya Chen: Recap — we'll send pilot pricing and SOW, Liam will run a quick benchmark, Priya will send sample prompts and dataset, Elena will request security docs. Any other asks?
[38:12] Priya Kapoor: Please add example guardrail rules for PII blocking and an example schema for our ticket payload.
[38:20] Maya Chen: Will do.

[40:00] Jordan Wu: I'll follow up with a short Console recording and links to docs (function calling, schema registry, Optimize guide).

[41:15] Daniel Ortiz: timeline-wise we are looking to pilot in April, production by mid-May if pilot goes well.
[41:25] Maya Chen: Great — we'll target benchmark next week and SOW by Friday.

[43:00] Sara Kim: thanks everyone, super helpful demo.
[43:04] Priya Kapoor: thanks.
[43:06] Liam Patel: Thanks all, we'll follow up.
[43:10] Maya Chen: bye everyone.
